From: Carlos Mendes <cmendes@veridianortho.com>
To: Anika Shah <ashah@veridianortho.com>
Cc: Dr. Leon Adeyemi <ladeyemi@veridianortho.com>
Date: Wed, 05 Sep 2018 10:18
Subject: Revised brochure claim: "proven long-term durability"

Anika,

For the 2019 ApexHip brochure refresh, I would like to add “proven long-term durability” to the opening spread, ideally alongside the large-head stability message.

We now have two years of strong sales growth and consistently positive feedback from the field, particularly from the active-patient surgeons. Feld’s group and several of the early adopters are telling us patients are doing very well, and the commercial team needs a clearer durability statement to keep the positioning ahead of the legacy metal-on-poly options.

Suggested copy:

“ApexHip is engineered for active adults, with proven long-term durability and stability designed to support a lifetime of movement.”

Leon, can you please review the supportability of “proven long-term durability”? I realize we do not yet have long-term Apex clinical or registry follow-up in the conventional sense, but the statement is intended to reflect the product’s performance to date, design rationale, and surgeon experience rather than a specific survivorship claim.

Anika, please have Kessler Reid work it into the next copy round pending Leon’s feedback. We should keep the language confident without turning the page into a data sheet.

Thanks,

Carlos

From: Carlos Mendes <cmendes@veridianortho.com>
To: Marcus Lee <mlee@veridianortho.com>; Jenna Whitfield <jwhitfield@veridianortho.com>; Anika Shah <ashah@veridianortho.com>
Date: Mon, 15 Nov 2021 10:18
Subject: Updated objection handling deck for national sales meeting

Marcus, Jenna, Anika—

For the national sales meeting, we have consolidated the field-facing objection handling materials into one updated deck: ApexHip_ObjectionHandling_NSM_v4.pptx.

The intent is to give the team a consistent, practical response framework rather than separate FAQs circulating by region. The deck includes:

• “metal ion” questions, including how to acknowledge monitoring concerns without speculating on individual clinical outcomes;
• the NJR and AJRR registry discussion, with approved context around the data and appropriate referral back to the treating surgeon;
• messaging on the label update and the October surgeon communication; and
• a short disclosure section for reps who are asked about KOL relationships, including Dr. Feld’s consulting/royalty arrangement and Dr. Rao’s advisory and speaker work.

Anika has coordinated the language and visuals so this stays aligned with the current Apex positioning and doesn’t read like a legal or regulatory script. We should be clear that the slides are discussion tools, not something to leave behind with customers.

Jenna, please have your district managers review before the regional breakouts and send any recurring questions by Thursday. Marcus, I’d appreciate your team reinforcing that improvising around registry numbers is not helpful.

Carlos

From: Carlos Mendes <cmendes@veridianortho.com>
To: Tom Halvorsen <thalvorsen@veridianortho.com>; Priya Raman <praman@veridianortho.com>
Date: Wed, 20 Feb 2019 14:22
Subject: RE: 55-degree wear retest results - concerning

Tom, Priya—

From a product-management perspective, a geometry change at this point would have a meaningful downstream impact. We have built the Apex positioning around stability, active patients, and “designed to last” performance. Reopening the hardware would affect that narrative as well as inventory, training, and the current launch plan.

Before we move to redesign, is there a path through surgical technique guidance? If the issue is principally elevated inclination, perhaps we reinforce the target range through the surgical guide, lab training, and field education rather than change the cup itself. Tom, I realize that may not resolve the engineering question, but it may be an appropriate interim control if the positioning relationship holds.

I agree we should raise this at the next design review, with Meridian’s input and whatever Priya can obtain from the Atlanta files. For now, please keep any discussion of this internal. We do not have enough context for a broader message.

Carlos

-----Original Message-----
From: Priya Raman <praman@veridianortho.com>
To: Tom Halvorsen <thalvorsen@veridianortho.com>; Carlos Mendes <cmendes@veridianortho.com>
Date: Wed, 13 Feb 2019 09:06
Subject: RE: 55-degree wear retest results - concerning

Tom—

I agree the result warrants a closer look, but I would be cautious about characterizing it as representative of field performance before we understand the test condition better.

The wear-test protocol approved at DR-3 specified 45° inclination, consistent with then-current practice and the protocol rationale in the DHF. Can you clarify whether 55° reflects a realistic surgical positioning distribution, versus a worst-case/outlier condition selected to challenge the construct? That distinction matters if we are considering any connection to complaints.

Please also loop Meridian Testing Labs in for an independent read of the setup, calculations, and interpretation before we escalate further. I do not want us to overreact to one retest without confirming reproducibility and clinical relevance.

I will review TW-2019-0417, including whether we have implant-position information in the Atlanta records. At present the complaint file has elevated metal ions and revision-related clinical notes, but I do not recall radiographic inclination being consistently captured. Per procedure, we can request any missing information from the reporting sites.

Carlos, please hold any external messaging until we have that additional context.

Priya

From: Greg Novak <gnovak@veridianortho.com>
To: Dr. Leon Adeyemi <ladeyemi@veridianortho.com>, Dana Okonkwo <dokonkwo@veridianortho.com>
Date: Wed, 14 Sep 2022 14:18:22 -0400
Subject: AJRR mid-2022 update - ApexHip still trending high

Leon, Dana,

I’ve finished pulling and reconciling the mid-2022 AJRR cumulative cut for our reconstruction portfolio.

The primary takeaway is that ApexHip continues to separate from the peer benchmark. The cumulative revision rate has ticked up further to 8.3% (up from the late 2021 figure), compared to the MoM class average holding relatively flat at 3.4%.

| Dataset / Cohort | Total Implants (n) | Revisions (n) | Cum. Revision Rate (%) | Class Avg MoM (%) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NJR (Mar 2021) | 1,842 | 131 | 7.1% | 3.2% |
| AJRR (Late 2021) | 2,910 | 224 | 7.7% | 3.3% |
| AJRR (Mid-2022) | 3,480 | 289 | 8.3% | 3.4% |

This trajectory aligns closely with the internal complaint volumes and TrackWise ARMD/metallosis escalations that Priya Raman’s team has been logging over the past two quarters. We are not looking at an anomaly or localized cluster. With this mid-2022 data, this pattern has now persisted across three consecutive registry reporting cycles: the UK NJR 2021 annual report, the late 2021 AJRR release, and now the mid-2022 AJRR dataset.

I strongly recommend that we include this updated registry table and survival curve in the briefing materials for the upcoming executive review of the Apex product line. While the October 2021 Dear Doctor letter and labeling update addressed surgical technique and inclination targeting, the cumulative registry curves are clearly continuing to climb rather than plateauing.

Let me know if you’d like me to walk through the underlying stratifications (head diameter vs. cup size) before the review.

Regards,

Greg Novak
Director, Post-Market Surveillance
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
ApexHip Surgeon Advisory Board
Meeting Minutes

Date: February 20, 2020
Location: Scottsdale, Arizona
Prepared by: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Subject: Scottsdale Advisory Board Minutes - Feb 2020

Attendees: Dr. Marcus Feld, Atlanta Joint Institute; Dr. Anita Rao, Nashville Hip & Knee; Dr. Leon Adeyemi, Chief Medical Officer; Marcus Lee, VP Sales, Reconstructive; Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip.

The group convened for the first day of the Scottsdale ApexHip advisory board session. Carlos reviewed 2019 utilization, with particular emphasis on continued growth in the active-adult segment and the role of large-head stability in surgeon adoption. Marcus noted that field enthusiasm remains strong, although reps are encountering more questions from hospital value-analysis committees regarding long-term comparative data.

Discussion then moved to the “Active Life” brochure and related surgeon-facing materials. Dr. Rao asked that the materials avoid language that could be read as promising a particular duration of implant survival. Dr. Adeyemi agreed that the message should stay focused on intended patient profile, stability, and the supporting clinical rationale rather than a broad longevity claim. Dr. Feld felt the patient imagery was effective but requested more practical discussion of return to recreational activity.

Carlos will take the brochure comments back to Marketing Communications and Kessler Reid. The physicians also requested updated data slides for use in educational programs, including current implant volume, available follow-up, and a clearer explanation of how the bearing differs from conventional metal-on-polyethylene systems. Dr. Adeyemi will review any clinical claims before the slides are circulated.

Dr. Feld raised that he has seen several earlier-than-expected revisions in his own practice, although he emphasized that the cases are not yet enough to draw a conclusion and may reflect patient selection, cup positioning, or follow-up patterns. He asked whether Veridian has seen similar observations elsewhere. Dr. Adeyemi stated that the clinical and complaint data should be reviewed in context and that individual revisions require case-level assessment. Dr. Rao recommended including updated revision and follow-up information in the next advisory-board data package.

Marcus Lee confirmed that the speaker bureau remains an important part of ApexHip education and that both Dr. Feld and Dr. Rao are expected to continue participating, subject to the usual program and compliance review. The group agreed that future programs should include adequate time for surgeon questions on patient selection and follow-up.

Compensation for the two-day advisory session was confirmed as follows:

| Physician | Session Days | Honorarium per Day | Total Honorarium |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Dr. Marcus Feld | 2 | $5,000 | $10,000 |
| Dr. Anita Rao | 2 | $5,000 | $10,000 |

Carlos will circulate revised Active Life messaging and a draft updated data deck for clinical review before the next speaker-program cycle.

From: Greg Novak
To: Dr. Leon Adeyemi; Dana Okonkwo; Priya Raman
Date: Fri, 17 Sep 2021 11:22
Subject: RE: Follow-up thoughts on the registry data

Leon, Dana,

Agree with your framing below — I don't think we're at "design defect" on the current evidence, but the direction of travel is what worries me more than any single number.

For what it's worth, I pulled the late-2021 AJRR extract yesterday. Sample size is much smaller than NJR (fewer years of Apex volume in the US registry, obviously), but the directional trend is consistent — elevated revision rate relative to class average, same general magnitude of gap. Not enough on its own to move the needle, but it doesn't contradict NJR either.

Given that, I'm going to build out a quarterly dashboard so we're not waiting on annual publication cycles to see where we stand — NJR and AJRR extracts side by side against class average, updated every quarter. I'll set a recurring calendar reminder for the pulls so it doesn't slip.

Priya — I'd like to loop you in once that's running so we can start correlating the registry trend against complaint volume/TrackWise data on our end. Will set up time next week.

Greg

-----Original Message-----
From: Dr. Leon Adeyemi
To: Dana Okonkwo; Greg Novak
Date: Tue, 16 Sep 2021 09:41
Subject: Follow-up thoughts on the registry data

Dana, Greg,

Wanted to put some additional thoughts down after Tuesday's meeting, mostly for my own clarity but also so we're aligned going forward.

The 7.1% five-year revision rate in the NJR report is genuinely concerning to me as a clinician, and I don't want that to get lost in how we're framing this internally. That said, I think we need to hold two possibilities open at once. The literature on edge-loading at high inclination angles is fairly consistent with what Tom's 2019 wear-test work showed at 55 degrees — and that pattern is often surgical-technique dependent rather than a pure implant design failure. Cup positioning variability across surgeons could be doing real work here, and that's not something a labeling change alone fixes, but it does mean I'm not ready to call this a design defect on the current data.

Given that, I support moving quickly on the labeling update — the sooner surgeons are reminded about inclination targets, the better. I'd also like us to pull PMS data again in six months rather than waiting for the next annual cycle.

I'm comfortable with continuing to sell under these conditions for now. But if the AJRR Q1 2022 numbers move in the wrong direction, I think we need to revisit this decision seriously.

Leon

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
INTERNAL MEMORANDUM

Date: January 10, 2019
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
To: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
Cc: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Subject: Proposal to re-run ApexHip wear testing at higher inclination angles

Priya, Carlos —

I want to formally propose a new round of wear testing on ApexHip at 55-degree cup inclination, and I'd like to get this scoped with Meridian Testing Labs sooner rather than later.

Some background for the file, though you both know most of this. Back at DR-3 in November 2016 we approved the wear-test protocol per ISO 14242 at the standard 45-degree inclination only. At the time that was defensible — it matched the predicate testing approach and the schedule didn't have room for a broader matrix. But in my 2017 post-launch monitoring memo I flagged that we should revisit inclination sensitivity about two years out, once we had real surgical placement data instead of bench assumptions. We're basically at that mark now.

Since launch I've been keeping an informal tracker of retrieval and imaging data where I can get it — mostly from explants and a few surgeon-shared fluoroscopy measurements, not a formal study, so treat it as directional. What it's showing is a meaningful cluster of cups implanted well outside the 45-degree target, some pushing 55 degrees or more, which is not surprising given how much placement varies case to case in the field. That's exactly the scenario our current test matrix doesn't cover.

I also can't ignore the Atlanta cluster Priya's team logged last August — three patients out of Dr. Feld's practice with elevated metal-ion complaints. I'm not saying inclination angle explains all three, and I know complaint handling is looking at this from the clinical side, but from a design standpoint it lines up with what edge-loading literature predicts: higher wear rates at higher inclination due to rim contact. If our bench testing has only ever validated the low end of the placement range surgeons are actually using, that's a gap we should close before it becomes a bigger problem.

Concretely, I'm asking for:

1. Budget approval for a supplemental wear-test run at 55-degree inclination, ISO 14242-based methodology, using the same head/cup combinations tested originally so we have a clean comparison.
2. Lab time with Meridian — I've had an informal conversation with their test engineer and they think they could slot us in by early Q2 if we commit soon.
3. Priya's team's input on what complaint/retrieval data would be useful to fold into the test rationale for the file.
4. Carlos, mainly a heads-up at this stage — I don't think this needs to touch messaging yet, but I wanted you looped in given any downstream implications for positioning if results come back different from the 45-degree data.

I'd estimate this is a $60–80K test program depending on sample size, plus lab turnaround of roughly 10–12 weeks. I know that's not trivial, but I'd rather we generate this data proactively than have it show up in a registry report or an FDA letter first.

Happy to walk through the tracker data in person if useful — I can bring the spreadsheet.

Tom

Date: April 9, 2020
Time: 10:00–10:50 AM
Location: Hub Conference Room "Reserve B" / Teams
Prepared by: Tom Halvorsen

Attendees: Tom Halvorsen (Sr. Design Engineer), Priya Raman (Director, Quality & Complaint Handling), Dana Okonkwo (VP Regulatory Affairs), Carlos Mendes (Product Manager, ApexHip)

1. Complaint Trend Update (Raman)

Priya walked through Q1 2020 TrackWise data. Metal-ion-related complaint volume (elevated Co/Cr, revision-for-pain, suspected ARMD) is now running 15-18 per quarter, up materially from the 2018 baseline of 3-4/quarter when the first Atlanta cluster was logged. Priya noted the increase tracks with growing implant population as much as anything, but the rate per 1,000 units in service is also trending up, not flat. She flagged this is consistent with what Tom's 2019 55-degree wear-test re-analysis predicted.

2. ECO-2019-118 Status (Halvorsen)

Tom confirmed the design change proposal (cup geometry / edge-loading mitigation) remains deferred per the 2019 design review decision. No new engineering work has been authorized since. Tom asked whether the updated complaint numbers change the calculus on revisiting it.

3. Discussion

Dana asked whether the complaint increase alone would trigger a design review reopening under our procedures; Priya said not automatically, but sustained upward trend plus registry data (NJR report expected later this year) could support it.

Carlos noted that 2020 is tracking to be Apex's best sales year yet — Q1 bookings are strong and the sales team is counting on continued momentum. He cautioned that any visible design-change activity, even internal, carries risk of leaking into the field and being read by surgeons or competitors as an admission of a problem, at a commercially sensitive moment. He was not opposed to engineering work continuing quietly but urged against any external-facing announcement or labeling change right now.

No consensus reached on reopening ECO-2019-118. Group agreed the complaint trend is worth continued close monitoring.

4. Action Items

- Raman to pull complete Q2 complaint data and re-run the trend comparison by mid-July.
- Halvorsen to keep wear-test analysis materials current in case design review is reopened.
- Group to reconvene after mid-year data to revisit whether ECO-2019-118 should move forward.
- Okonkwo to monitor for any external registry publications in the interim.

Rachel,

Attached is the draft 21 CFR Part 806 recall notification package prepared for submission to CDRH regarding the voluntary recall of ApexHip acetabular cups.

Per our discussion with Bill Kowalski and Quality, the key elements summarized in the submission document are as follows:

1. Root Cause: Adhesion failure of the porous titanium KinetiCoat layer attributed to plasma-spray parameter drift following scheduled vacuum chamber maintenance at the Cork facility.
2. Scope / Lot Range: Acetabular cup lots V-2200 through V-2299, manufactured in Cork between November 2021 and February 2022.
3. Distribution Data: 1,140 total units distributed commercially; based on hospital reconciliation and registry cross-referencing to date, 412 units have been implanted.
4. Health Hazard Evaluation & Classification: Proposing a voluntary Class II classification. The risk assessment concludes that while unbonded coating flaking upon opening presents a delay in surgery or potential local inflammatory response if introduced, the probability of serious adverse health consequences remains low.

We are targeting an official submission date to the FDA district office in early June, prior to the planned formal customer notification and initiation date of June 14, 2022.

Please review the attached formal notification letter and let me know if legal has any required edits. I would appreciate your sign-off by end of day Friday, May 27, so Devon can finalize the submission packet.

To: Priya Raman <praman@veridianortho.com>; Carlos Mendes <cmendes@veridianortho.com>
Subject: Engineering Status Review: ECO-2019-118 (Apex Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry & Clearance) — Closing the Loop

MEMORANDUM

TO: Priya Raman, Director of Quality & Complaint Handling; Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
FROM: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
DATE: January 10, 2022
SUBJECT: Engineering Status Review: ECO-2019-118 (Apex Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry & Clearance) — Closing the Loop

I am writing to formally revisit the open engineering posture surrounding ECO-2019-118. It has now been nearly three years since I submitted the initial Engineering Change Order proposal in February 2019, and our Design History File (DHF) index still does not accurately capture where we stand on this.

To recap the technical history: during the development phase leading up to Design Review 3 (DR-3) in November 2016, our wear simulator protocol was established strictly under ISO 14242-1 standard parameters, testing acetabular component placement at a nominal 45° inclination angle only. The Meridian Testing Labs reports confirmed acceptable volumetric wear under those ideal, nominal conditions, which supported our 510(k) clearance (K162447). However, as I flagged in my February 2019 re-analysis memo, testing the system under steeper acetabular cup inclinations—specifically 55°—produced severe edge-loading dynamics. The wear simulator data showed a 4× to 6× increase in gravimetric and volumetric metal wear rates compared to the 45° baseline, driven by localized contact stresses at the cup rim during microseparation cycles.

ECO-2019-118 proposed an immediate modification to the acetabular rim radius and polar clearance profile to mitigate edge-loading wear at non-ideal cup angles (which clinical data shows occur frequently in real-world patient anatomy).

In mid-2019, leadership decided to formally defer ECO-2019-118. The stated rationale at the time centered on commercial friction: tooling changeout costs, scrap write-downs, and especially the timeline required for full mechanical and simulator requalification, which would have disrupted peak production volumes.

Here is my primary concern today: as of January 2022, three full years after we identified the 4–6× wear multiplier under steep angles, no design change has been implemented. None. The product currently being shipped from Warsaw and Cork retains the exact rim geometry cleared in 2017.

Furthermore, I reviewed the ApexHip DHF index in Agile last week and noticed ECO-2019-118 is marked as "Closed / Superseded by Commercial Labeling Review." This is factually incorrect and creates an audit vulnerability. The engineering risk was never resolved or designed out; it was *deferred*. We should not be relying solely on post-market technique guides or surgeon education to manage a mechanical wear condition that we know occurs once the cup tilts past 50°.

I recommend two immediate corrective actions:
1. Re-open the DHF index entry for ECO-2019-118 and formally designate its status as "Deferred — Pending Clinical Registry / Post-Market Review," explicitly noting that the original ISO 14242 protocol tested only 45° inclination and did not evaluate edge-loading conditions.
2. Reconvene the cross-functional engineering review team (Quality, Product Management, R&D) to decide whether we are going to requalify the modified rim tooling or leave the deferred status on the permanent record.

We have known about the edge-loading wear multiplier since early 2019. Leaving the change order in administrative limbo without a clear engineering resolution is a significant unaddressed risk.

Regards,

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

Subject: 55-degree wear retest results - concerning

Priya, Carlos—

I re-ran the ISO 14242 wear simulation at 55° cup inclination rather than the 45° orientation used in the DR-3 protocol. Results are attached: Apex_wear_55deg_rev2.xlsx.

Short version: this is not a marginal difference.

At 55°, the wear rate is 4–6x higher than the 45° baseline depending on head/cup combination. The damage is concentrated at the cup rim, with visible edge-loading/scoring rather than the more uniform pattern we saw under the original setup. Co/Cr debris generation tracks with that increase.

I know 55° is not the nominal surgical target, but it is not an exotic placement angle either. We have always known inclination varies in the field. Testing only at 45° gave us a clean result, but it does not appear to represent this condition.

Priya: I think we need to look at the Atlanta metal-ion cluster in TrackWise against cup position if we have radiographs or surgeon notes. This result could explain at least part of what is being reported there. I am not saying every elevated-ion complaint is this mechanism, but the correlation is concerning enough that we should not treat it as routine complaint noise.

Carlos: please do not turn this into a messaging exercise yet. First we need a design review. I want to discuss whether the cup geometry/rim needs to change, and whether there are interim limitations we should be considering.

Can we convene DR-4 this week? This is urgent, not a normal protocol follow-up.

Tom

Re: Recall Closure Request — Z-1418-2022, ApexHip Acetabular Cup Lots V-2200–V-2299

To Whom It May Concern:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. respectfully requests termination of recall status for the voluntary Class II recall initiated June 14, 2022, identified by FDA Recall Number Z-1418-2022.

The recall applied to ApexHip acetabular cups, lots V-2200 through V-2299, manufactured at our Cork, Ireland facility and distributed in the United States. A total of 1,140 units were distributed. As of October 14, 2022, all but a small number of units have been retrieved or otherwise accounted for through customer inventory reconciliation and documented disposition. The remaining units are with accounts that have provided written confirmation that the affected product is no longer available for use and has been quarantined pending final return processing.

Recall notifications were issued to all direct accounts, distributors, and consignees. Veridian conducted follow-up communications and effectiveness checks in accordance with 21 CFR Part 7. The final effectiveness-check response rate was 98.6%; nonresponding accounts were subject to repeated outreach and inventory verification through their purchasing or materials-management departments.

The underlying issue was identified as plasma-spray parameter drift following chamber maintenance. Corrective and preventive action CAPA-2022-0091 addressed chamber requalification requirements, parameter controls, operator verification, and enhanced incoming inspection. CAPA effectiveness checks have been completed and passed. Review of post-implementation production and inspection records did not identify recurrence of coating adhesion failures.

Two MDR reports related to Denver operating-room cases involving affected product were submitted to FDA under 21 CFR Part 803. Both reports have been acknowledged by FDA.

Based on completion of notification, product recovery and accountability activities, and verified corrective action effectiveness, Veridian requests that FDA terminate the recall status for Z-1418-2022. Supporting records are available upon request.

Sincerely,

Dana Okonkwo
Vice President, Regulatory Affairs
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

Subject: Draft "Dear Doctor" Letter – ApexHip Acetabular System Labeling Update

MEMORANDUM

TO: Dana Okonkwo (VP, Regulatory Affairs), Rachel Steinberg (General Counsel), Dr. Leon Adeyemi (Chief Medical Officer), Marcus Lee (VP, Sales)
FROM: Carlos Mendes (Product Manager, ApexHip)
DATE: September 28, 2021
SUBJECT: Draft "Dear Doctor" Letter – ApexHip Acetabular System Labeling Update

Following the decisions reached during our September 14 Registry Signal Review meeting, I have prepared the initial draft text for the upcoming customer notification ("Dear Doctor" letter) regarding the ApexHip Total Hip System.

As agreed by the review team and executive leadership, Veridian will maintain active commercial distribution of ApexHip while implementing an immediate Instructions for Use (IFU) labeling update to address emerging registry trends.

Background & Signal Summary
The primary driver for this communication is data presented from the March 2021 National Joint Registry (NJR) 17th Annual Report, which identified a cumulative 5-year revision rate of 7.1% for the ApexHip construct, compared to an average class benchmark of approximately 3.2% across contemporary metal-on-metal (MoM) hip resurfacing and total replacement systems. While internal clinical evaluations indicate that well-positioned constructs continue to demonstrate strong clinical survivorship, registry data and internal engineering assessments correlate early revisions predominantly with adverse local tissue reactions (ALTR/ARMD) linked to elevated cobalt and chromium ion levels.

Proposed Letter Content & Labeling Guidance
The draft notification emphasizes patient safety, precise surgical technique, and targeted post-operative vigilance:

1. Patient Monitoring Recommendations: We advise clinicians to establish heightened routine clinical and radiographic follow-up protocols for all implanted ApexHip patients, with particular attention to individuals receiving larger femoral head diameters (≥44 mm). Routine cross-sectional imaging (MARS-MRI or ultrasound) and periodic blood metal-ion quantification (whole blood cobalt and chromium) should be considered annually or upon any presentation of unexplained pain, clicking, or swelling.
2. Surgical Positioning & Angle Inclination: Revisions strongly correlate with edge-loading phenomena. The revised labeling explicitly instructs surgeons to target an acetabular cup inclination angle within 40° to 45° and anteversion between 15° and 20°. Operating outside these ranges—specifically exceeding 50° of operative abduction—markedly increases the risk of accelerated fluid-film wear and premature component loosening.

Next Steps & Timeline
Our target mail date to all US and EU implanting orthopedic surgeons, chief medical officers, and relevant risk management personnel is mid-October 2021. Reps will receive accompanying talking points once this text is locked.

Please review the attached formal notification layout (`Apex_Dear_Doctor_Draft_v1.docx`) and provide your redlines. We require formal sign-off from Regulatory Affairs, Legal, and Clinical before Dana submits the final package to the agency and we proceed with mass distribution.

From: Tom Halvorsen <thalvorsen@veridianortho.com>
Sent: Monday, January 10, 2022 9:14 AM
To: Priya Raman <praman@veridianortho.com>; Carlos Mendes <cmendes@veridianortho.com>
Subject: Engineering Status Review: ECO-2019-118 (Apex Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry & Clearance) — Closing the Loop

MEMORANDUM

TO: Priya Raman, Director of Quality & Complaint Handling; Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
FROM: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
DATE: January 10, 2022
SUBJECT: Engineering Status Review: ECO-2019-118 (Apex Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry & Clearance) — Closing the Loop

I am writing to formally revisit the open engineering posture surrounding ECO-2019-118. It has now been nearly three years since I submitted the initial Engineering Change Order proposal in February 2019, and our Design History File (DHF) index still does not accurately capture where we stand on this.

To recap the technical history: during the development phase leading up to Design Review 3 (DR-3) in November 2016, our wear simulator protocol was established strictly under ISO 14242-1 standard parameters, testing acetabular component placement at a nominal 45° inclination angle only. The Meridian Testing Labs reports confirmed acceptable volumetric wear under those ideal, nominal conditions, which supported our 510(k) clearance (K162447). However, as I flagged in my February 2019 re-analysis memo, testing the system under steeper acetabular cup inclinations—specifically 55°—produced severe edge-loading dynamics. The wear simulator data showed a 4× to 6× increase in gravimetric and volumetric metal wear rates compared to the 45° baseline, driven by localized contact stresses at the cup rim during microseparation cycles.

ECO-2019-118 proposed an immediate modification to the acetabular rim radius and polar clearance profile to mitigate edge-loading wear at non-ideal cup angles (which clinical data shows occur frequently in real-world patient anatomy).

In mid-2019, leadership decided to formally defer ECO-2019-118. The stated rationale at the time centered on commercial friction: tooling changeout costs, scrap write-downs, and especially the timeline required for full mechanical and simulator requalification, which would have disrupted peak production volumes.

Here is my primary concern today: as of January 2022, three full years after we identified the 4–6× wear multiplier under steep angles, no design change has been implemented. None. The product currently being shipped from Warsaw and Cork retains the exact rim geometry cleared in 2017.

Furthermore, I reviewed the ApexHip DHF index in Agile last week and noticed ECO-2019-118 is marked as "Closed / Superseded by Commercial Labeling Review." This is factually incorrect and creates an audit vulnerability. The engineering risk was never resolved or designed out; it was *deferred*. We should not be relying solely on post-market technique guides or surgeon education to manage a mechanical wear condition that we know occurs once the cup tilts past 50°.

I recommend two immediate corrective actions:
1. Re-open the DHF index entry for ECO-2019-118 and formally designate its status as "Deferred — Pending Clinical Registry / Post-Market Review," explicitly noting that the original ISO 14242 protocol tested only 45° inclination and did not evaluate edge-loading conditions.
2. Reconvene the cross-functional engineering review team (Quality, Product Management, R&D) to decide whether we are going to requalify the modified rim tooling or leave the deferred status on the permanent record.

We have known about the edge-loading wear multiplier since early 2019. Leaving the change order in administrative limbo without a clear engineering resolution is a significant unaddressed risk.

Regards,

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

MEMORANDUM

TO: Dana Okonkwo (VP, Regulatory Affairs), Rachel Steinberg (General Counsel), Dr. Leon Adeyemi (Chief Medical Officer), Marcus Lee (VP, Sales)
FROM: Carlos Mendes (Product Manager, ApexHip)
DATE: September 28, 2021
SUBJECT: Draft "Dear Doctor" Letter – ApexHip Acetabular System Labeling Update

Following the decisions reached during our September 14 Registry Signal Review meeting, I have prepared the initial draft text for the upcoming customer notification ("Dear Doctor" letter) regarding the ApexHip Total Hip System.

As agreed by the review team and executive leadership, Veridian will maintain active commercial distribution of ApexHip while implementing an immediate Instructions for Use (IFU) labeling update to address emerging registry trends.

Background & Signal Summary
The primary driver for this communication is data presented from the March 2021 National Joint Registry (NJR) 17th Annual Report, which identified a cumulative 5-year revision rate of 7.1% for the ApexHip construct, compared to an average class benchmark of approximately 3.2% across contemporary metal-on-metal (MoM) hip resurfacing and total replacement systems. While internal clinical evaluations indicate that well-positioned constructs continue to demonstrate strong clinical survivorship, registry data and internal engineering assessments correlate early revisions predominantly with adverse local tissue reactions (ALTR/ARMD) linked to elevated cobalt and chromium ion levels.

Proposed Letter Content & Labeling Guidance
The draft notification emphasizes patient safety, precise surgical technique, and targeted post-operative vigilance:

1. Patient Monitoring Recommendations: We advise clinicians to establish heightened routine clinical and radiographic follow-up protocols for all implanted ApexHip patients, with particular attention to individuals receiving larger femoral head diameters (≥44 mm). Routine cross-sectional imaging (MARS-MRI or ultrasound) and periodic blood metal-ion quantification (whole blood cobalt and chromium) should be considered annually or upon any presentation of unexplained pain, clicking, or swelling.
2. Surgical Positioning & Angle Inclination: Revisions strongly correlate with edge-loading phenomena. The revised labeling explicitly instructs surgeons to target an acetabular cup inclination angle within 40° to 45° and anteversion between 15° and 20°. Operating outside these ranges—specifically exceeding 50° of operative abduction—markedly increases the risk of accelerated fluid-film wear and premature component loosening.

Next Steps & Timeline
Our target mail date to all US and EU implanting orthopedic surgeons, chief medical officers, and relevant risk management personnel is mid-October 2021. Reps will receive accompanying talking points once this text is locked.

Please review the attached formal notification layout (`Apex_Dear_Doctor_Draft_v1.docx`) and provide your redlines. We require formal sign-off from Regulatory Affairs, Legal, and Clinical before Dana submits the final package to the agency and we proceed with mass distribution.

Re: Notification of Labeling Update – ApexHip Total Hip System
510(k) K162447

To Whom It May Concern:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. is providing notice of a voluntary labeling update for the ApexHip Total Hip System, cleared under 510(k) K162447 on March 9, 2017.

Following Veridian’s September 14, 2021 Registry Signal Review, the Company elected to clarify the Instructions for Use and surgeon-facing labeling regarding patient follow-up and monitoring where postoperative cup inclination angles are high. This action follows review of post-market registry information, including the March 2021 annual report of the United Kingdom National Joint Registry (NJR), which reported a five-year revision rate of 7.1% for ApexHip compared with a 3.2% class average.

The revised labeling will include the following clarification:

1. Surgeons should consider postoperative radiographic assessment of acetabular component position, including inclination angle, as part of routine clinical follow-up.

2. For patients with high cup inclination angles, physicians should consider closer clinical follow-up and evaluation for symptoms potentially associated with elevated metal ion exposure or adverse local tissue reaction.

3. Where clinically indicated, evaluation may include serum cobalt and chromium testing, cross-sectional imaging, and/or referral for additional assessment consistent with the treating physician’s clinical judgment.

The update does not alter the device’s indications for use, contraindications, materials, manufacturing process, sterilization method, intended use, or design specifications. No physical change has been made to the ApexHip Total Hip System. The revision is intended to provide additional clarification to surgeons based on post-market information and does not represent a design change.

Veridian has assessed the labeling revision under 21 CFR 807.81(a)(3) and FDA’s guidance regarding when to submit a new 510(k) for a change to an existing device. Veridian concludes that a new premarket notification is not required because the change is limited to labeling clarification and does not affect safety or effectiveness in a manner that could significantly affect the device’s safety or effectiveness, nor does it constitute a major change or modification in intended use.

We intend to distribute the revised Instructions for Use and an accompanying Dear Doctor communication to ApexHip customers during October 2021. The revised labeling and supporting assessment have been retained in the ApexHip design history file.

Please contact me if the Office of Compliance has questions or requires additional information.

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
INTERNAL MEMORANDUM

Date: June 11, 2020
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
To: ApexHip Design History File
Re: Status of ECO-2019-118 (Acetabular Cup Edge-Loading Design Change) — Deferred

Purpose

This memo documents the current status of engineering change order ECO-2019-118 for inclusion in the ApexHip design history file. I'm writing this now because it's been over a year since the wear test data came in and the change is still sitting on the shelf, and I want a clear record of where things stand and why.

Background

In February 2019 I re-ran wear testing at 55° cup inclination (our original DR-3 protocol only tested at the standard 45° per ISO 14242). Results showed 4-6x higher volumetric wear at the higher inclination angle compared to nominal. I sent these findings to Priya Raman and Carlos Mendes at the time, and we opened ECO-2019-118 to evaluate a bearing surface / cup geometry modification to reduce edge-loading sensitivity at higher inclination angles, which we know from literature and our own cadaver lab work is a realistic range for a meaningful subset of surgical placements, not an edge case.

Current status

The ECO was scoped and a preliminary design concept (revised cup rim geometry, option B in the working file) was drafted by March 2019. Since then it has not progressed. As of this memo:

1. No formal risk assessment update has been completed tying the 55° wear data to clinical outcome risk.
2. Resource allocation has gone to KneeFlex line extensions and sustaining engineering on the stem, per R&D prioritization set in Q2 2019 and reaffirmed since.
3. Quality has not escalated this to a CAPA or design review gate, and to my knowledge no closure or cancellation decision has been formally documented — it is simply inactive.
4. I've raised status verbally at two design review touchpoints (Sept 2019, Jan 2020) without a decision either way.

Recommendation

Given that we now have over a year of additional complaint volume in TrackWise referencing metal-ion levels and early revision, and given that registry attention (I understand Greg's group is tracking NJR data closely) appears to be trending in a direction consistent with what the 55° testing predicted, I recommend this decision be formally revisited rather than left in limbo. Specifically, I'd like to see:

- A documented risk assessment addressing the 55° findings against current complaint/registry signal, owned by Quality or RA, not just Engineering.
- A go/no-go decision on ECO-2019-118 made at a design review with sign-off, whatever that decision ends up being.

I want to be clear that I am not asserting a safety conclusion here — that's outside my lane and above my pay grade to make alone. What I am asserting is that this deferral has been driven by resourcing and prioritization, not by a documented determination that the wear data doesn't matter. That distinction should be captured in the file.

Please route this memo into the DHF under the ECO-2019-118 folder.

— Tom Halvorsen

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. submits this formal response to the Additional Information (AI) request dated December 12, 2016, regarding premarket notification K162447 for the ApexHip Total Hip System.

Regarding Question 3 concerning the wear simulator test protocol:

The pre-clinical wear assessment for the ApexHip acetabular cup and femoral head articulation was conducted strictly in accordance with ISO 14242-1 (*Implants for surgery — Wear of total hip-joint prostheses — Part 1: Loading and displacement parameters for wear-testing machines and corresponding environmental conditions for test*) and ISO 14242-2 (*Part 2: Methods of measurement*).

Testing was executed by Meridian Testing Labs under Protocol MTL-2016-W702 (Final Report MTL-TR-8841-A, dated October 14, 2016). Testing utilized the standard anatomical acetabular cup inclination angle of 45°, which directly aligns with the established testing parameters historically approved for our predicate device, the ClassicHip System (K081942).

Veridian Orthopedics maintains that simulator testing conducted at the standardized 45° inclination provides a robust, clinically relevant baseline sufficient to establish substantial equivalence. Gravimetric wear rates demonstrate that the ApexHip bearing couple exhibits superior wear performance relative to the legally marketed predicate.

Summary wear-rate data across 5.0 × 10⁶ cycles are provided below:

* ClassicHip System Predicate (36 mm Co/Cr Head / UHMWPE Cup): 14.65 ± 1.42 mg / 10⁶ cycles (K081942 Verification Report VR-07-22)

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
MEETING MINUTES

Meeting: Apex Coating Issue Field Action Decision Meeting
Date: April 21, 2022
Time: 10:00–11:15 a.m. ET
Location: Teams / Warsaw Hub, Conference Room 4B
Prepared by: Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs

Attendees: Dana Okonkwo, Priya Raman, Bill Kowalski, Rachel Steinberg, Carlos Mendes, Owen Park

Purpose
To review the KinetiCoat adhesion issue affecting certain ApexHip acetabular cup lots and determine the appropriate field action.

Discussion Summary

Mr. Kowalski reviewed Cork manufacturing records and the preliminary investigation. The affected population is cup lots V-2200 through V-2299, manufactured following the plasma-spray chamber maintenance event. The current evidence supports parameter drift during the relevant production period as the probable cause of insufficient KinetiCoat adhesion. The observed failure mode is coating flaking or separation identified on unwrapping during incoming inspection at two hospital customers.

Ms. Raman confirmed that the distribution reconciliation currently identifies 1,140 affected units distributed. Of those, 412 are recorded as implanted. The remaining units are believed to be in hospital inventory, distributor inventory, or otherwise pending confirmation through the effectiveness process. Quality will continue reconciliation as customer responses are received.

The group agreed that the product should be removed from distribution and that a voluntary Class II recall is warranted for lots V-2200 through V-2299. Regulatory will proceed on that basis, subject to final review of the notification package and lot list.

For avoidance of doubt, the scope of this field action is limited to the KinetiCoat adhesion/manufacturing issue associated with the identified cup lots. Metal-ion levels, wear performance, ARMD, registry data, and other metal-on-metal concerns were expressly noted as outside the scope of this action. Those matters are being addressed through their respective Quality, Post-Market Surveillance, and Regulatory processes and should not be characterized in customer communications as the basis for this recall.

Ms. Okonkwo advised that the target for recall initiation should be mid-June 2022, allowing time for completion of the health hazard evaluation, final lot tracing, customer lists, and FDA notification materials. Ms. Steinberg requested that communications remain factual and limited to the identified coating adhesion condition, the affected lots, and the customer instructions.

Mr. Mendes noted that Sales will require a concise field script and FAQ once the customer letter is approved. Ms. Raman stated that the initial hospital notification should instruct customers to identify, quarantine, and return unused affected cups, while providing a contact path for questions regarding implanted devices. No clinical recommendation language will be included without Regulatory and clinical review.

Mr. Park confirmed that Finance will begin modeling the anticipated reserve, including return logistics, replacement product, customer notification, and potential claim exposure. He asked Quality to provide a weekly update on the distributed/implanted reconciliation.

Action Items

1. Dana Okonkwo — Draft FDA voluntary recall notification, health hazard evaluation, and associated Regulatory package. Target: May 6, 2022.
2. Priya Raman — Prepare hospital notification letter, distribution list, return instructions, and effectiveness-check process. Target: May 13, 2022.
3. Bill Kowalski — Complete Cork batch-record review and provide final affected-lot confirmation and root-cause documentation. Target: April 29, 2022.
4. Owen Park — Begin financial reserve modeling based on 1,140 distributed units and 412 implanted units; update as reconciliation changes. Target: May 6, 2022.
5. Carlos Mendes — Prepare draft Sales FAQ and field communication plan after Quality/Regulatory approve customer language. Target: May 20, 2022.

SUBJECT: Litigation Reserve Recommendation — ApexHip Product Liability (Q2 2023)

Rob, Rachel:

Following our preliminary review of Q1 close figures and in light of external developments over the past six weeks, Finance recommends an immediate adjustment to the product liability reserve established for ApexHip. Specifically, we recommend increasing the existing $18.0M accrual established in Q3 2022 by $8.0M, bringing the total litigation reserve to $26.0M effective for the Q2 2023 financial statements.

Basis for Reserve Adjustment

As discussed with Whitfield & Barr last month, the service of the initial state-court complaints in late March represents a formal transition from an unasserted potential liability to active litigation. The underlying clinical exposure cited in these initial filings tracks precisely with the registry data we reviewed internally throughout 2021:

1. NJR 7.1% 5-Year Revision Rate: The initial complaints heavily quote the March 2021 NJR annual report benchmark (7.1% vs. 3.2% class average) as prima facie evidence of elevated failure.
2. AJRR Corroboration: Late-2021 AJRR registry metrics, which demonstrated parallel divergence in domestic revision curves, have now been incorporated into plaintiff filings regarding ARMD and elevated cobalt/chromium ion levels.

Given the rate of initial filings and discussions with outside counsel regarding potential consolidation scenarios, Hannah Berg and I modeled defense costs, potential initial settlement valuations, and retention liabilities under our Aegis Specialty policy. As you know, Aegis issued a reservation of rights last year, meaning defense expense erosion will fall heavily within our direct retention before excess coverage responds. An accrual of $26.0M aligns more closely with probable and reasonably estimable losses under ASC 450.

Commercial Impact & Top-Line Drag

The legal exposure continues to compound top-line erosion. The commercial fallout from the registry disclosures, the October 2021 surgeon notification, and the residual confusion from the unrelated 2022 cup coating recall has severely impaired Apex reorder rates.

Hannah’s FP&A team has completed the updated spring forecast. ApexHip annualized revenue for FY2023 has been revised downward again, dropping from our prior budget projection of $54M to approximately $42.0M annualized. This represents a significant contraction from peak 2020 revenue ($96M) and will create an operational margin drag of roughly 180 bps across Reconstructive.

Please let me know when we can take 15 minutes to align before I brief the Audit Committee ahead of the May board meeting.

Short version: we traced it back to the chamber maintenance we did in early November after the plasma torch nozzle swap. Line techs recalibrated afterward but the post-maintenance verification run wasn't tight enough to catch a drift in the spray parameters - specifically powder feed rate and standoff distance crept outside the validated window for about a 12-week window before it got flagged in incoming inspection at the two hospitals. Batch records confirm the drift lines up with lots in that range, nothing before or after.

Proposed corrective actions:
1. Revised preventive maintenance checklist for the plasma spray chamber, adding explicit parameter checks post-maintenance, not just equipment function checks.
2. Mandatory calibration verification run with witness coupons before the line restarts production after any chamber maintenance event, sign-off required by both line lead and quality.
3. Tightened SPC alarm limits on feed rate and standoff distance so we catch drift earlier next time.

Want to flag clearly - this is a coating/manufacturing issue on the Cork line, root cause is process drift after maintenance. It's not related to the wear/metal-ion tracking Priya's team has going separately on the complaint side. Different animal entirely, just want to make sure that distinction stays clear in the CAPA file.

Let me know if you want changes before I route this for QA sign-off.

Bill

Date: November 15, 2022
From: Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs
Subject: Recall Closure Memorandum - Z-1418-2022, ApexHip Acetabular Cup Lots V-2200-V-2299

This memorandum documents final reconciliation and recommended closure of Veridian Orthopedics’ voluntary Class II recall of ApexHip acetabular cup lots V-2200 through V-2299 (FDA Recall No. Z-1418-2022).

The recall was initiated on June 14, 2022, following reports from two hospital incoming-inspection locations of KinetiCoat coating flaking on cups removed from their sterile packaging. The affected lots were manufactured at the Cork facility between November 2021 and February 2022. The field action applied only to the identified acetabular cup lots and was not associated with post-market reports concerning metal ion levels, wear, or ARMD.

Final distribution reconciliation is as follows:

| Disposition | Units |
|---|---:|
| Total units distributed | 1,140 |
| Confirmed implanted before recall notification | 412 |
| Returned to Veridian / distributor inventory | 681 |
| Customer-destroyed with documentation received | 47 |
| Total recovered or otherwise accounted for | 728 |

All 1,140 distributed units have now been reconciled through documented implantation status, return, or customer-certified destruction. Recall effectiveness checks, including follow-up to non-responding accounts and distributor verification, reached a final effectiveness rate of 98.6% after reconciliation. The remaining 1.4% represents accounts for which receipt of the recall communication was confirmed through alternate records, including shipment, email delivery, and distributor contact documentation, but a completed response form was not obtained despite repeated follow-up.

The investigation concluded that the coating adhesion condition resulted from plasma-spray parameter drift following an October 2021 chamber maintenance event at the Cork facility. Specifically, the chamber was returned to production without adequate confirmation that operating parameters remained within validated ranges for application of the KinetiCoat porous titanium coating. Batch records and retained-sample review supported the conclusion that the issue was limited to the affected lot range.

Corrective and preventive actions were managed under CAPA-2022-0091. Actions included recertification of Chamber 3, revalidation of the applicable plasma-spray operating window, enhanced verification following maintenance activity, revised maintenance-release documentation, and tightened process-control review requirements for coating runs. Quality has verified implementation and effectiveness of these actions. CAPA-2022-0091 is now closed.

Regulatory Affairs recommends that the FDA District Office be notified that recall effectiveness activities and final reconciliation are complete, with closure requested for Recall No. Z-1418-2022. Recall records, including customer notifications, response records, distribution and return reconciliation, investigation materials, CAPA documentation, and FDA correspondence, should be retained in accordance with 21 CFR 806.20. The DHF-linked recall file should be archived in Agile with cross-references to the Cork manufacturing investigation and CAPA-2022-0091.

Dana

National Sales Meeting 2018
ApexHip Positioning Deck — Speaker Notes

Presenter: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Date: January 18, 2018
Session: Reconstructive Portfolio Breakout
Distribution: Field Sales and Marketing

Slide 1 — Why Apex, Why Now

Open with the patient, not the bearing. The ApexHip patient is generally an active adult who expects to remain active: working, traveling, cycling, golf, family life. We have an opportunity to offer a modern total hip platform designed around stability, range of motion, and durable materials.

Do not frame ClassicHip as a bad product. It remains an important, proven option and is appropriate for many patients. The positioning is choice: ClassicHip is our established metal-on-poly platform; ApexHip gives the surgeon another option for the active, appropriately selected patient who values a large-head construct and a contemporary fixation platform.

Suggested line: “Apex expands the conversation beyond simply getting back to walking. It is designed for the patient who wants confidence in movement.”

Slide 2 — Differentiating the Platform

The three pillars are:

1. Stability through large-head options. Apex offers head sizes from 36 to 50 mm, allowing surgeons to select a construct that supports stability and range of motion.

2. Wear performance. In our ISO 14242 bench testing at standard 45-degree cup inclination, Apex demonstrated lower early wear rates than legacy systems. Keep this statement tied to the test conditions and use the approved leave-behind if a surgeon asks for data.

3. Fixation. The acetabular cup uses KinetiCoat porous titanium coating, acquired with KBT, to support bone ingrowth and initial fixation.

Avoid getting drawn into a head-to-head “winner” discussion with every competitor. We do not need to name brands to make the point. Most competitive systems can offer a large head or porous coating; Apex brings those features together in a coherent system backed by Veridian’s reconstructive organization.

Slide 3 — KinetiCoat: Make It Concrete

Reps should be comfortable explaining the coating in plain language. KinetiCoat is not paint and should never be described that way. It is a porous titanium coating applied to the cup surface to create a structure intended to support bone ingrowth over time.

Suggested language: “The goal is biologic fixation. KinetiCoat gives the surgeon a porous surface designed to help the patient’s bone engage with the cup.”

Do not overstate this as faster healing, guaranteed fixation, or superior fixation in every patient. Use “designed to support” and “intended to promote” consistently.

Slide 4 — Handling the Longevity Question

This is important: do not promise a specific number of years. We have bench data and a strong engineering rationale, but clinical follow-up for Apex is still short. Do not tell a surgeon or patient that Apex will last 20 years, 25 years, or “a lifetime.”

If asked, say: “Apex was designed with durability in mind, and the available bench testing supports its wear-performance profile. As with any newer system, long-term clinical follow-up continues to accumulate.”

Do not substitute a ClassicHip survivorship number for an Apex claim. The products are different, and surgeons will notice.

Slide 5 — Close

The ask is simple: identify the right surgeon and the right patient profile, lead with stability, wear performance at the validated test condition, and KinetiCoat fixation advantages. Be confident, be specific, and stay within the approved language.

If a question goes beyond the materials in the field guide, do not improvise. Send it to Product Marketing or Clinical Affairs and we will get an answer back quickly.

MEMORANDUM

Date: 12 April 2022
From: Bill Kowalski, Plant Manager, Cork
To: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs
Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Subject: Preliminary Root Cause Assessment — KinetiCoat Adhesion Failures, Cup Lots V-2200 through V-2299

Priya, Dana, Tom —

Following up on the two incoming-inspection complaints (Northgate Health System and the Denver facility) regarding flaking of the KinetiCoat porous titanium coating on unwrapped acetabular cups, the line investigation team here has completed our preliminary root cause review. I want to get this in front of you before we go further so we can talk timing on any containment action.

Background: on 18 November 2021 we performed scheduled preventive maintenance on plasma-spray chamber 2 (the chamber used for essentially all cup coating runs from that date forward). Part of that maintenance involved replacement of the torch nozzle assembly and recalibration of the gas flow controllers. Our post-maintenance verification at the time checked flow rates and confirmed the chamber was "in spec" per the standard startup checklist, but that checklist does not independently verify chamber temperature ramp behavior or the standoff distance (nozzle-to-substrate gap) under sustained production conditions — only at idle. Our engineering team's review of the process data historian shows a slow drift in both chamber temperature (running roughly 15–20°C above the historical mean during long runs) and standoff distance (drifting outward by approximately 1.5–2 mm from the qualified setpoint) beginning almost immediately after the November maintenance and continuing undetected until the chamber was next serviced in early February 2022.

This drift window corresponds closely to production of cup lots V-2200 through V-2299.

Bond strength testing (per our internal pull-test method, spec minimum 20 MPa) on retained samples pulled from the affected date range confirms the concern. Results below.

Lot / Test Bond Strength
V-2214 / 13.1 MPa
V-2231 / 12.0 MPa
V-2248 / 14.6 MPa
V-2267 / 11.8 MPa
V-2284 / 15.3 MPa
V-2192 (pre-drift, control) / 26.4 MPa
V-2305 (post-repair, control) / 24.9 MPa

As you can see, every affected lot we've pulled samples from tests well below the 20 MPa specification, with values as low as 11.8–12.0 MPa. Lots manufactured before the November maintenance event and after the February re-service both test comfortably in the 24–28 MPa range, consistent with our historical process capability. This is a strong signal that the maintenance event itself is the root cause, not a raw material or supplier issue — incoming titanium powder lots for this period test within normal specification and show no anomalies.

We have not yet identified why the post-maintenance verification checklist failed to catch the drift; that's a separate CAPA item on our end and I'll have more for you on the checklist gap by end of month.

Recommendations:

1. Quarantine all remaining Cork and Warsaw inventory of cup lots V-2200 through V-2299 pending final disposition. I've already instructed the warehouse here to segregate what we have on-site.
2. Priya, I'd ask Quality to coordinate with Dana's team on whether this warrants a field action given units already distributed — 1,140 units went out the door in this lot range per our shipping records, and we don't yet know how many are implanted.
3. Tom, if you have bandwidth, it would help to have Design confirm there's no interaction between the coating adhesion issue and the wear characteristics you've been looking at — I want to be clear these appear to be independent failure modes, but I know that question will come up.

I'll have the full root cause report, including corrective action plan for chamber 2 monitoring going forward, by the end of next week. Happy to get on a call before then if useful.

Bill

Bill Kowalski
Plant Manager, Cork
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

This memo summarizes ApexHip complaint trending for Q3 2019 (July–September) per Complaint Handling Procedure QSP-014, and provides a comparison against Q1 and Q2 2019 volumes.

2. Complaint Volume Summary

Total ApexHip complaints logged in TrackWise for Q3 2019: 9. Of these, 4 are classified as suspected metal-ion/wear-related (elevated cobalt/chromium, pain, or suspected ARMD presentation), consistent with the pattern first identified in the Atlanta cluster (TW-2018-0311, TW-2018-0312, TW-2018-0319). New complaints of note this quarter:

- TW-2019-0402 — Nashville, Dr. A. Rao's practice. Patient presenting with groin pain at 22 months post-implant; elevated serum cobalt reported by treating physician. Investigation ongoing.
- TW-2019-0417 — Denver, reporting surgeon Dr. J. Whitaker. Patient with joint effusion and suspected pseudotumor on imaging; revision surgery scheduled. Explant tissue requested per procedure.

(a) continued monthly trending review of ApexHip complaints per standard cadence;
(b) a follow-up periodic re-review of the metal-ion-pattern cluster at the close of Q4 2019, incorporating any explant findings from TW-2019-0417 and TW-2019-0402; and

Subject: Literature scan supporting registry signal ahead of September meeting

Dana, Greg,

Ahead of the Registry Signal Review next month, I pulled together a brief scan of the orthopedic literature examining edge-loading wear mechanisms and systemic cobalt/chromium ion elevation in large-diameter metal-on-metal systems.

There are clear published parallels to what Greg is tracking in the NJR dataset and the steep wear gradient Tom Halvorsen documented in his 2019 simulator re-analysis at elevated cup abduction angles (>50°). In particular, the clinical community has documented that when steep acetabular inclination induces stripe wear and micro-separation, local tissue necrosis and pseudotumor formation correlate heavily with serum Co and Cr spikes, even before frank mechanical loosening shows up on radiographs.

I strongly recommend our presentation packet explicitly reference at least two foundational papers—likely Hart et al. (JBJS 2012) on edge loading and ion thresholds, and Langton et al. (BJJ 2011) regarding component positioning and bearing diameter.

Regardless of whether the committee leans toward continuing commercial distribution under an updated surgical technique and tighter labeling guidance (e.g., rigid cup positioning safe zones to mitigate steep inclination) or favors a more conservative action, our clinical rationale must be defensible against the external peer-reviewed consensus. We cannot appear to evaluate the registry revision curve in an epidemiological vacuum.

I will distill these citations into a one-page summary table for Greg to include with the pre-read materials.

Best regards,

Leon

This assessment reflects information available through April 2023 and should be updated as registry, complaint, and litigation information develops.

2. Registry and clinical information

The March 2021 UK National Joint Registry annual report identified an ApexHip five-year revision rate of 7.1%, compared with a 3.2% class average. Subsequent AJRR information received in late 2021 was directionally consistent with a higher-than-expected revision signal, although the available datasets differ in patient mix, follow-up duration, and reporting completeness.

The principal clinical concern is adverse reaction to metal debris associated with elevated cobalt and chromium ion levels in a subset of patients, including patients revised for soft-tissue findings. The data do not establish that every early revision is attributable to metal debris or that all implanted devices present the same risk. Nonetheless, the registry signal warranted, and continues to warrant, enhanced surveillance.

Dr. Leon Adeyemi has reviewed the available clinical information and remains of the opinion that continued availability is supportable at this time with appropriate patient selection, surgeon awareness, and post-market follow-up. His view is that the large-head MoM construct may continue to offer stability benefits for selected patients, provided that surgeons consider cup positioning, contraindications, symptoms, imaging findings, and metal-ion testing where clinically indicated. Dr. Adeyemi has emphasized that this is not a conclusion that the observed revision trend is acceptable without continued monitoring.

3. September 2021 decision and field actions

At the September 14, 2021 Registry Signal Review, management considered the NJR and preliminary AJRR information, complaint data, clinical input, and commercial considerations. The decision was to continue distribution while strengthening labeling and physician communications rather than withdraw ApexHip from the market.

The resulting labeling update and October 2021 Dear Doctor letter addressed patient selection, component positioning, follow-up expectations, and evaluation of patients presenting with pain or other symptoms potentially associated with metal debris. Sales and clinical personnel were instructed to use the approved materials and not to characterize the registry findings as disproven or immaterial.

The decision remains defensible only if the enhanced controls are maintained and the supporting data are reviewed at defined intervals. Post-Market Surveillance should continue its registry and complaint trending reviews, with escalation to Regulatory Affairs, Quality, Clinical, and senior management if material changes are identified.

4. June 2022 coating recall

The June 14, 2022 voluntary Class II recall, FDA Recall No. Z-1418-2022, involved acetabular cup lots V-2200 through V-2299 manufactured in Cork. That action concerned KinetiCoat adhesion failures, including coating flaking observed upon unwrapping at customer sites. The identified root cause was plasma-spray parameter drift following a chamber maintenance event.

This was a manufacturing/coating matter distinct from the metal-ion wear and ARMD concerns reflected in the registry data and state-court allegations. The affected population was limited to the identified cup lots; 1,140 units were distributed and 412 were implanted. Communications should continue to preserve this distinction while recognizing that external parties may seek to associate the two matters.

5. Regulatory considerations

Veridian remains obligated to evaluate reportable events and submit MDRs as required under 21 CFR Part 803. Complaint handling and trending must remain timely, documented, and consistent with established procedures. The 2021 FDA inspection observation regarding complaint-trending timeliness remains relevant to execution discipline.

At present, Regulatory Affairs does not recommend a market-status change based on the available information. However, continued adverse registry trends, a meaningful increase in confirmed ARMD-related revisions, new clinical evidence, or an adverse regulatory development could change that recommendation promptly. We should not represent that the current actions eliminate risk.

6. Reserve and litigation outlook

An $18 million reserve for Apex-related claims was recorded in Q3 2022. Mr. Park’s team is reviewing the adequacy of that reserve in light of current claim activity, expected additional state-court filings, defense costs, and potential insurance recoveries. While no multidistrict proceeding has yet been formed, management should plan for the possibility that the growing volume of cases could result in coordinated federal litigation later in 2023.

The reserve analysis should remain separate from the clinical and regulatory assessment, while recognizing that further adverse registry information or a change in market status may affect both assumptions.

7. Recommendation

No change in ApexHip market status is recommended at this time. Continued availability should be conditioned on enhanced surveillance, disciplined complaint and MDR evaluation, adherence to updated labeling and surgeon communications, and recurring executive review of registry and revision data. A reassessment should occur promptly if the adverse trend persists or worsens.

Dana

With the NJR report showing that 7.1% 5-year revision rate, I went back into Agile and pulled my wear-simulator re-analysis memo from February 2019 (file was Apex_wear_55deg_rev2.xlsx / memo ref TM-19-004).

If you remember, when we ran the simulator at a 55-degree cup inclination angle instead of the standard 45-degree setup specified in ISO 14242 (which is what we used for the original DR-3 design verification back in late 2016), volumetric wear shot up by 4x to 6x. The edge-loading was pretty dramatic once you tipped past 50 degrees, and the ion release curves followed the exact same slope.

At the time, we drew up ECO-2019-118 to modify the rim clearance geometry, but leadership deferred the change because the 510(k) cleared envelope was based on the 45-degree test data and nobody wanted to reopen testing or delay manufacturing.

Given what the UK registry is putting out now, I think we have to revisit whether deferring that design change was the right call. The clinical numbers match what we saw on the bench almost down to the decimal.

I can put together a clean 3-page summary of the 2019 data before the signal review group convenes. Let me know if you want me to write that up or just walk through the raw simulator curves.

Re: Notification of Voluntary Market Withdrawal – ApexHip Total Hip System

To Whom It May Concern:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. is providing notice that it intends to voluntarily withdraw the ApexHip Total Hip System from the United States market effective February 2, 2024.

ApexHip is a metal-on-metal total hip system cleared under 510(k) K162447 on March 9, 2017. The product includes cobalt/chromium femoral components and a cobalt/chromium acetabular cup with KinetiCoat porous titanium coating. Veridian will cease U.S. commercial distribution of ApexHip on the effective date and will communicate the withdrawal to affected customers, distributors, and surgeon users.

This action follows Veridian’s assessment of the totality of available post-market information regarding the system’s metal-ion and wear performance profile. That assessment includes the UK National Joint Registry annual report issued in March 2021, which identified a five-year ApexHip revision rate of 7.1 percent compared with a 3.2 percent class average, as well as subsequent American Joint Replacement Registry trends that raised similar concerns. Veridian has also considered clinical complaint information, including reports involving elevated cobalt and chromium ion levels, adverse reaction to metal debris, and early revision procedures.

In addition, Veridian is aware that multidistrict litigation concerning ApexHip was formed in December 2023. While the litigation is ongoing and no conclusions should be drawn from this notice regarding any particular allegation or claim, its formation is among the circumstances considered in Veridian’s decision to discontinue commercial availability of the system.

This voluntary market withdrawal is separate from Veridian’s June 14, 2022 voluntary Class II recall of certain ApexHip acetabular cup lots, V-2200 through V-2299, under FDA Recall Number Z-1418-2022. That recall addressed a manufacturing-related KinetiCoat adhesion issue associated with plasma-spray parameter drift at the Cork facility. The present withdrawal does not concern that coating issue. Rather, it addresses the distinct metal-ion/wear performance profile identified through registry, complaint, and other post-market data.

Veridian does not recommend prophylactic revision solely as a result of this market withdrawal. Patients with implanted ApexHip systems should continue routine clinical follow-up as determined by their treating surgeon, including evaluation and monitoring based on the patient’s symptoms, clinical presentation, and surgeon judgment. Veridian will continue to meet its complaint handling, medical device reporting, and other post-market surveillance obligations under applicable requirements, including 21 CFR Parts 803 and 820.
